lessons.title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
body: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Dodgson, an Oxford mathematics lecturer who first told the story to the daughters of a college colleague on a boat trip in 1862. The book appeared in 1865 and broke from earlier children's books, which mostly taught morals. It plays with logic, language, and Victorian manners, and it shows how Victorian children memorized and recited verse.

lessons.title: The Jungle Book
body: Rudyard Kipling, who was born in India, published these linked stories in 1894. They include Mowgli, a boy raised by wolves, and other tales such as Rikki-Tikki-Tavi. The stories were written during British rule in India, and some of their attitudes reflect that time.

lessons.title: Little Women
body: Louisa May Alcott published Little Women in 1868 and 1869, drawing on her own sisters and her father's unusual household in Massachusetts. It follows the four March sisters while their father is away serving in the Civil War. It was a rare book that treated girls' ambitions seriously.

lessons.title: Treasure Island
body: Robert Louis Stevenson published Treasure Island in 1883 after serializing it as "The Sea Cook" in a boys' magazine. Narrated by young Jim Hawkins, it set many images of pirates, such as treasure maps, a one-legged sailor, and a parrot, that later stories repeated. Long John Silver is one of literature's great morally mixed characters.

lessons.title: Oliver Twist
body: Charles Dickens published Oliver Twist in installments between 1837 and 1839, shortly after England's 1834 Poor Law reform created harsh workhouses. It follows an orphan who escapes the workhouse and falls in with London pickpockets led by Fagin. Dickens used it to criticize how society treated poor children.

lessons.title: A Christmas Carol
body: Charles Dickens published A Christmas Carol on December 19, 1843, in a year when Britain faced widespread poverty and child labor. He wrote it quickly, and it helped shape how English-speaking people celebrate Christmas. It is divided into five "staves," like verses of a song.

lessons.title: The Three Musketeers
body: Alexandre Dumas published the novel as a newspaper serial in 1844, setting it two centuries earlier in the reign of Louis XIII, when Cardinal Richelieu held enormous power. It follows the young Gascon d'Artagnan, who comes to Paris hoping to join the King's Musketeers. Many characters were based on real people from the period, mixed with invention.

lessons.title: Around the World in Eighty Days
body: Jules Verne published this novel in 1872-1873, after new technology such as steamships, transcontinental railways, and the Suez Canal had made world travel faster. Phileas Fogg wagers that he can circle the globe in eighty days. The book reflects how the British Empire and fast communication were shrinking the world.

lessons.title: Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea
body: Jules Verne published the novel in 1869-1870, when submarines were primitive and the deep ocean was largely unknown. Captain Nemo's Nautilus was an imagined machine far ahead of its time. The book is told by Professor Aronnax, who is captured and carried through the world's seas.

lessons.title: The Call of the Wild
body: Jack London published the book in 1903, drawing on his own time in the Klondike Gold Rush of 1897-1898. Buck, a pampered California dog, is stolen and sold to work as a sled dog in the north. The story follows his change from a domestic pet into a creature of the wild.

lessons.title: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer
body: Mark Twain published the novel in 1876, drawing on his own boyhood in Hannibal, Missouri, which he renamed St. Petersburg. It is set before the Civil War in a river town where slavery existed. The story follows Tom through pranks, a murder he witnesses, and an adventure in a cave.

lessons.title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
body: Arthur Conan Doyle collected twelve Holmes stories in 1892 after they first appeared in The Strand Magazine. Narrated by Dr. Watson, they follow the detective Sherlock Holmes in a fast-changing London of gaslight, trains, and telegrams. The stories helped shape the modern detective story.

lessons.title: Pride and Prejudice
body: Jane Austen published Pride and Prejudice in 1813, during the Regency, when a gentry daughter without an inheritance had few ways to secure her future except marriage. The novel follows the Bennet family, whose estate is entailed away from the five daughters. It mattered because it joined sharp social comedy to a love story driven by character rather than rank.

lessons.title: Frankenstein
body: Mary Shelley began Frankenstein at nineteen, during a rainy 1816 summer near Lake Geneva, and published it anonymously in 1818. It was written as science was exploring electricity and the nature of life, and it is often called an early work of science fiction. The story is framed by letters from an Arctic explorer, Robert Walton, which hold Victor Frankenstein's and the creature's accounts.

lessons.title: A Tale of Two Cities
body: Charles Dickens published A Tale of Two Cities in weekly installments in 1859, setting it during the French Revolution and the Reign of Terror. The story contrasts London and Paris and draws on Dickens's reading of Thomas Carlyle's history of the revolution. It is one of Dickens's only two historical novels and opens with the famous line about the best of times and the worst of times.

lessons.title: Dracula
body: Bram Stoker published Dracula in 1897, when Victorians were anxious about invasion, disease, and changing roles for women. The novel is told through diaries, letters, newspaper clippings, and phonograph recordings, showing that the characters fight an old monster with modern tools like shorthand, typewriters, and blood transfusion. It established many of the vampire conventions later films used.

lessons.title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
body: Mark Twain published Huckleberry Finn in 1884 (in the U.S. in 1885), setting it decades earlier along the Mississippi when slavery was legal. Narrated by an uneducated boy in regional dialect, it was groundbreaking in using vernacular American speech. It is both celebrated and debated for its satire of racism and for its use of period slurs.

lessons.title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
body: Oscar Wilde first published The Picture of Dorian Gray in a magazine in 1890 and expanded it into a novel in 1891. It belongs to the Aesthetic movement, which argued for "art for art's sake," and was criticized by contemporaries as immoral. The preface gathers Wilde's sayings about art and morality.

lessons.title: Jane Eyre
body: Charlotte Bronte published Jane Eyre in 1847 under the pen name Currer Bell, and it was an immediate success. It is narrated by Jane, an orphan who becomes a governess, and it blended romance, Gothic mystery, and social criticism at a time when women had few paths to independence. Its first-person confession was bold for its day.

lessons.title: Wuthering Heights
body: Emily Bronte published Wuthering Heights in 1847 under the pen name Ellis Bell, and critics at first found it shocking. The story is set on the wild Yorkshire moors over two generations and is told through nested narrators, chiefly the housekeeper Nelly Dean and the tenant Mr. Lockwood. It was Emily's only novel.

lessons.title: Romeo and Juliet
body: William Shakespeare wrote Romeo and Juliet in the 1590s, drawing on an older Italian tale, and the first printing appeared in 1597. It was performed at the Globe-era London theaters, where all parts were played by men and boys. The play mixes comedy and tragedy and is written in a blend of verse and prose, including a sonnet in its opening speech.

lessons.title: Hamlet
body: Shakespeare wrote Hamlet around 1600, and early printed versions appeared in 1603 and 1604. It is based on an older Scandinavian legend of a prince avenging his father. It is Shakespeare's longest play and is known for its soliloquies, speeches in which a character speaks his thoughts aloud.

lessons.title: Great Expectations
body: Charles Dickens serialized Great Expectations in weekly installments in 1860 and 1861. It follows Pip, an orphan raised by his sister and her blacksmith husband, who comes into a mysterious fortune. The novel explores class mobility in Victorian England and is told by the grown Pip looking back.

lessons.title: The Count of Monte Cristo
body: Alexandre Dumas published this novel in newspaper installments in 1844-1846. It is set during the turbulent years after Napoleon's fall, when Bonapartists and royalists struggled for power in France. Its huge serial audience made it one of the best-selling adventure novels ever written.

lessons.title: Les Misérables
body: Victor Hugo wrote the novel largely while in exile from Napoleon III's France and published it in 1862. It follows ex-convict Jean Valjean through the decades after Waterloo, ending around the Paris uprising of 1832. Hugo used the story to argue that poverty and a harsh legal system create "miserables".

lessons.title: Sense and Sensibility
body: Jane Austen's first published novel appeared anonymously in 1811, "By a Lady". Under the inheritance laws of the time, the Dashwood sisters lose their home to a male relative and must rely on marriage and connections. The novel shows how tightly money and reputation controlled women's choices.

lessons.title: Emma
body: Jane Austen published Emma in 1815, setting it entirely in and around the village of Highbury. Austen herself said she was creating a heroine whom "no one but myself will much like". The story shows how a wealthy young woman's confidence in her own judgment leads her into comic and painful mistakes.

lessons.title: The War of the Worlds
body: H. G. Wells published the novel in 1897-1898, when Britain ruled a vast empire. He flipped the usual story by imagining a more advanced power invading England and treating humans as the colonized. The book helped create the modern alien invasion story.

lessons.title: The Time Machine
body: H. G. Wells published this short novel in 1895, drawing on Darwin's theory of evolution and worries about the gap between rich and poor in industrial Britain. The Time Traveller visits the year 802,701 and finds two descendants of humanity: the gentle Eloi and the underground Morlocks. It is one of the founding works of science fiction.

lessons.title: The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
body: Robert Louis Stevenson published this short novel in 1886, in a London that prized respectability and hidden private vice. The story is told through the eyes of lawyer Mr. Utterson, who slowly uncovers the link between the respected Dr. Jekyll and the brutal Mr. Hyde. It became so famous that "Jekyll and Hyde" is now a phrase for a split personality.

lessons.title: The Importance of Being Earnest
body: Oscar Wilde's comedy premiered in London in 1895 and was subtitled "A Trivial Comedy for Serious People". Two friends invent false identities to escape their duties, and the play mocks Victorian ideas about respectability and marriage. It was a huge hit, but Wilde's scandal and trial soon ended his career.

lessons.title: The Metamorphosis
body: Franz Kafka, a German-speaking Jewish writer in Prague, published the novella in 1915. It opens with salesman Gregor Samsa waking to find himself changed into a giant insect, and the story never explains why. The book is a landmark of modernist and absurdist writing.

lessons.title: The Scarlet Letter
body: Nathaniel Hawthorne published the novel in 1850, setting it in seventeenth-century Puritan Massachusetts, a community ruled closely by religion. Hester Prynne is punished for adultery and made to wear a scarlet letter A. The book explores guilt, secrecy, and the harsh judgment of a strict society.

lessons.title: The Odyssey
body: The Odyssey is attributed to Homer and was performed aloud for centuries before it was written down. It tells of Odysseus's ten-year journey home after the Trojan War, while his wife Penelope and son Telemachus hold out against suitors in Ithaca. Greek ideas of hospitality, called xenia, shape nearly every episode.

lessons.title: The Art of War
body: Traditionally credited to Sun Tzu, a Chinese general, this short text was written during a long period of conflict among rival Chinese states. It advises that the best victory is won without fighting and that war should be avoided if possible. It is read today in military, business, and political settings.

lessons.title: Moby Dick
body: Herman Melville published Moby-Dick in 1851, drawing on his own time aboard a whaling ship in the 1840s. At that time whaling was a major American industry, and whale oil lit lamps across the country. The novel failed commercially at first and was recognized as a masterpiece only after Melville's death.

lessons.title: Crime and Punishment
body: Fyodor Dostoevsky serialized Crime and Punishment in 1866 in a Russian journal, setting it in the poor districts of St. Petersburg. It follows Raskolnikov, a former student who murders a pawnbroker, believing extraordinary people may break moral rules. Dostoevsky himself had been sentenced to prison in Siberia and drew on that experience.

lessons.title: War and Peace
body: Leo Tolstoy published War and Peace between 1865 and 1869. It follows several aristocratic Russian families through Napoleon's campaigns, including the 1812 invasion and the burning of Moscow. It blends fictional characters with real events and argues about what really causes history.

lessons.title: Anna Karenina
body: Leo Tolstoy serialized Anna Karenina from 1875 to 1877 and published it as a book in 1878. It interweaves the story of Anna, a married aristocrat who has an affair, with that of Levin, a landowner seeking purpose. It opens with the famous line that all happy families are alike while each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.

lessons.title: Don Quixote
body: Miguel de Cervantes published the first part of Don Quixote in 1605 and the second in 1615. It follows an old gentleman who reads so many chivalric romances that he sets out as a knight-errant, with his squire Sancho Panza. It is often called the first modern novel and a parody of the knightly tales that were then popular.

lessons.title: The Iliad
body: The Iliad is attributed to Homer and covers a few weeks in the tenth year of the Trojan War. It opens with the rage of Achilles after Agamemnon takes his prize and follows the death of Patroclus and Hector. It was composed in an oral tradition and became the foundation of Greek education and literature.

lessons.title: Middlemarch
body: George Eliot, the pen name of Mary Ann Evans, published Middlemarch in installments in 1871-1872. It is set in a Midlands town around the time of the First Reform Act of 1832. Interwoven plots show the lives of Dorothea Brooke, Dr. Lydgate, and others, and the book is often called one of the greatest English novels.
